unit.title: Scams and how to spot them
unit.description: Unauthorised firms, Ponzi schemes, pump and dump, phishing, finfluencers and what to do if you get scammed

steps.title: What a «chiringuito» is
steps.body:
A firm that offers investment services **without authorisation** (in Spain they're called «chiringuitos financieros»). They usually have very professional websites, English-sounding names and very friendly «advisers».

Every year the CNMV (Spain's securities regulator) publishes hundreds of **warnings** about unauthorised firms.

steps.title: The red flags
steps.body:
1. They contact you **out of the blue**.
2. They promise **high, guaranteed** returns.
3. They **rush** you.
4. They ask you to install **remote access** software (AnyDesk, TeamViewer).
5. They ask for transfers to other countries or in crypto.
6. You see your balance grow, but you **can't withdraw it** without first paying «taxes» or «fees».

steps.title: Always check
steps.body: Before investing, look the firm up on **cnmv.es**: in the registers of authorised firms and in the warnings list. Never trust what its own website says.
steps.key: If someone contacts you unprompted offering high, safe returns, it's almost certainly a scam.
steps.tip: Nobody who knew a safe way to make 20 % a month would call you up to tell you about it.

steps.title: How they work
steps.body:
A **Ponzi scheme** pays early investors with money from new ones. There's no real business behind it, or hardly any. As long as new money keeps coming in, everything seems to be going brilliantly.

A **pyramid scheme** does the same, but you earn mainly by **recruiting** others.

When the new money stops, it collapses.

steps.title: Real cases
steps.body:
• **Charles Ponzi**, Boston, 1920: he promised 50 % in 45 days.
• **Bernard Madoff**, uncovered in 2008: for decades he fooled even professional investors.
• **Fórum Filatélico and Afinsa**, Spain, 2006: hundreds of thousands of victims of a stamp business.

steps.title: Impossible returns
steps.body: 1 % a day sounds small, but compounded it multiplies your money by 37 in a year. 10 % a month is more than 200 % a year. Nothing legal delivers that consistently.
steps.key: If the maths doesn't work with compound interest, it isn't a business: it's a scam.

u32l3.title: Pump and dump and signal groups

steps.title: How it works
steps.body:
**Pump and dump**:

1. The organisers quietly buy a small asset (a crypto or a thinly traded share).
2. They announce it as «the signal» on Telegram, WhatsApp or social media.
3. Members buy and the price shoots up.
4. The organisers sell at the top.
5. The price crashes and the latecomers lose.

steps.title: Why it's a trap
steps.body: It's **market manipulation**, banned on stock exchanges and, under the EU's MiCA regulation, in crypto too. And «VIP signals» groups that charge a fee usually make money from your fee and your purchase, not from getting calls right.
steps.key: If you're tipped off at the same time as thousands of people, you're not the one buying early: you're the one buying high.

steps.title: The variants
steps.body:
• **Phishing:** an email pretending to be your bank, the tax office or a delivery company.
• **Smishing:** the same by text message.
• **Vishing:** a call from a fake bank employee.
• **Spoofing:** they fake the sender or the number so it looks official.

They're all after the same thing: your passwords, your codes or getting you to make a transfer.

steps.title: The golden rules
steps.body:
• Your bank will **never** ask for your full passwords or SMS codes by phone, email or message.
• Don't tap links in unexpected messages: go into the app or website yourself.
• Turn on **two-step verification**.
• When you're being rushed («your account will be blocked in 1 hour»), stop and check.

steps.title: If you've already fallen for it
steps.body: Call your bank on its official number to block the card or the transaction, change your passwords and report it. You can get help on **017**, the free cybersecurity helpline run by INCIBE (Spain's national cybersecurity institute).
steps.key: No bank will ever ask for your passwords or codes: whoever asks for them is robbing you.

steps.title: What they can and can't do
steps.body:
An influencer can **explain concepts** and share their experience. What they **can't** do without CNMV authorisation is **advise you**: tell you what to buy based on your situation.

If they're paid to talk about a product, they have to make it clear that it's **advertising**.

steps.title: Crypto and advertising
steps.body: Since 2024, crypto-asset advertising in the EU has been regulated by **MiCA**: it must be **clear, fair and not misleading**, be identified as advertising and warn about the risks. The CNMV replaced its old circular (1/2022) with 1/2024 to adapt. And its guide for finfluencers points out that writing «this isn't advice» **doesn't protect you** if in practice you're making recommendations.

steps.title: Questions to ask yourself
steps.body: Do they make money if I buy? Do they show me their losses or only their wins? Are they selling me a course or «signals»? Are they rushing me? Lots of followers doesn't mean they know how to invest.
steps.key: An influencer can teach you; if they tell you what to buy, ask yourself who's paying them.

steps.title: What to do right now
steps.body:
1. **Don't send any more money**, even if they promise to return what you've already paid.
2. **Tell your bank** as soon as possible: sometimes a transfer can be stopped or the card blocked.
3. **Keep evidence:** screenshots, chats, emails, payment receipts, websites.
4. **Report it** to the Policía Nacional or the Guardia Civil.
5. **Notify the CNMV** if it was an unauthorised firm.

steps.title: Where to complain
steps.body:
• Against an **authorised** firm (broker, bank): first to its customer service department; if they don't side with you, to the **CNMV** (investments) or the **Banco de España** (banking and payments).
• For cybersecurity questions: INCIBE's **017**, free and confidential.

steps.title: Watch out for the second scam
steps.body: After a scam come the fake «recovery firms»: they promise to get your money back in exchange for an upfront fee. They're the same people, or people just like them.
steps.key: Stop the damage, keep evidence and report it. And be wary of anyone offering to recover your money in exchange for money.
steps.tip: Getting scammed doesn't make you stupid: it makes you human. Reporting it helps stop it happening to someone else.

u32l1-1.prompt: Select all the messages that come from an unauthorised firm.
options: Your annual tax report is now available in the app.
Your balance is €14,250. To withdraw it, you first need to pay €1,900 in taxes.
To help you with your account I need you to install AnyDesk. That way I can set it up for you 😊
Hi, I'm Daniel from Global Prime Invest. We've got a forex opportunity with a guaranteed 4 % a month. Shall we talk today?
Remember: we'll never ask for your passwords by phone or message.
u32l1-1.explanation: Unsolicited contact, guaranteed returns, remote access and «pay to withdraw»: the four classic red flags.

u32l1-2.prompt: Put in order how to check a firm before giving it money.
options: Look it up in the official registers on cnmv.es
Check the CNMV's warnings list
If it isn't authorised, don't invest
Write down its exact name and website
u32l1-2.explanation: Always on the CNMV website, never on the firm's own.

options: A fund with lots of fees
A cheap broker
A firm that offers investments without authorisation
u32l1-3.explanation: It can have a flawless website and still not be authorised.

u32l1-4.prompt: Which ones are red flags? Select all that apply.
options: You can't withdraw your balance without paying first
Very high guaranteed returns
It appears as authorised in the cnmv.es registers
They ask you to install remote access software
u32l1-4.explanation: Being authorised in the official registers is what a legal firm should have (although that doesn't guarantee an investment will go well).

u32l1-5.prompt: If a company has a professional website and an office in London, it's a legal firm.
options: True
False
u32l1-5.explanation: Websites get copied and addresses get made up. Only the official registers can confirm it.

u32l1-6.prompt: Someone called Marcos from «Atlas Capital Partners» rings you. He offers 5 % a month in forex, «today only», and asks for €250 to open the account. What do you do?
options: Hang up and look the name up on the CNMV
Give it a go with €250, it's not much
Ask him to email me a contract
u32l1-6.explanation: 5 % a month is almost 80 % a year. Nobody serious offers that over the phone.
feedback: Good: unsolicited contact, impossible returns and pressure. Three red flags in one go.
That's how it starts: next come the calls to «make the most of it» and pay in more.
A nice-looking contract doesn't make it legal. Check the authorisation.

u32l1-7.prompt: To check whether a firm is authorised, search the ____ website.
options: AEAT
OCU
DGT
CNMV
u32l1-7.explanation: The Comisión Nacional del Mercado de Valores supervises investment services in Spain.

u32l1-8.prompt: Quick: an «adviser» asks you to install AnyDesk to help you invest. What do you do?
options: Hang up: it's a classic scam signal
Just give them my bank password
Install it, it'll be quicker
u32l1-8.explanation: With remote access they can use your online banking as if they were you.

u32l1-9.prompt: If a firm appears on the CNMV's warnings list, it means it isn't authorised.
options: True
False
u32l1-9.explanation: That list exists precisely to warn about unauthorised firms.

u32l1-10.prompt: What do you say to Lumi?
options: Sign up, you might get lucky
Don't tap it: look the platform up on the CNMV and be wary of that profile
Give her your details so she can help you
u32l1-10.explanation: Unsolicited contact + impossible returns = scam, even if it comes with a smile.
feedback: 3 % a day doesn't exist: it's a textbook scam, often with a fake profile.
Nice! «Friends» who end up recommending a platform are a very common scam.
Your details are exactly what they're after.
lines: A really nice girl messaged me on Instagram 😍
She says she makes 3 % a day on a platform and sent me the link.

u32l2-1.prompt: How does a Ponzi scheme pay its early investors?
options: With money paid in by new investors
With government loans
With profits from a real business
u32l2-1.explanation: That's why it needs new money coming in non-stop.

u32l2-2.prompt: A website promises 1 % a day, compounded. If it were true, what would €1,000 grow into in 365 days? (round it)
u32l2-2.explanation: 1,000 × 1.01³⁶⁵ ≈ €37,783. No real investment does that: it's the sign of a Ponzi.

u32l2-3.prompt: Another one promises 10 % a month. Compounded, what annual return would that be? (round it)
u32l2-3.explanation: 1.1¹² ≈ 3.14 → +214 % a year. Global stock markets have averaged 5.2 % a year after inflation over 125 years.

u32l2-4.prompt: Select the messages that smell like a Ponzi or a pyramid scheme.
options: Fixed return of 2 % a week. Our traders never lose.
Your deposit at 2 % APR matures on 15 March.
Return over the last year: −4 %. Past performance is no guarantee of future returns.
Pay €300 to join and earn €100 for every friend you bring. With 10 friends you reach gold level!
u32l2-4.explanation: Earning by recruiting and sky-high fixed returns with no explanation of where they come from are their typical signs.

u32l2-5.prompt: Is it more typical of a Ponzi or a pyramid scheme?
options: You earn mainly by bringing in new members
Sky-high fixed returns with no explanation of where they come from
There are levels depending on how many people you recruit
They say they invest your money in something secret and very profitable
u32l2-5.explanation: Both need new money to pay the old investors; what changes is the hook.

u32l2-6.prompt: A friend of Laura's made 15 % in two months in an «investment club» and shows her the payments. She keeps pushing Laura to join now. What does Laura do?
options: She's suspicious, asks where the returns come from and looks the club up on the CNMV
She puts in all her savings to make money faster
She joins: the payments are real
u32l2-6.explanation: Payments to the first investors are a Ponzi's bait.
feedback: Good: someone getting paid proves nothing. A Ponzi pays out until the money stops coming in.
If it's a Ponzi, whoever joins late is the one who loses everything.
In a Ponzi the first ones really do get paid, with money from those who come later.

u32l2-7.prompt: Charles Ponzi promised a 50 % return in 45 days.
options: True
False
u32l2-7.explanation: Boston, 1920. His name has been tied to this fraud ever since.

u32l2-8.prompt: A Ponzi scheme pays old investors with money from ____.
options: banks
fund managers
dividends
new investors
u32l2-8.explanation: When new ones stop arriving, the house of cards collapses.

u32l2-9.prompt: What did the Bernard Madoff case, uncovered in 2008, show?
options: That a Ponzi can last decades and fool professional investors
That Ponzi schemes only fool beginners
That the CNMV exposed it in Spain
u32l2-9.explanation: He delivered suspiciously steady returns year after year. Too regular is also a red flag.

u32l2-10.prompt: Fórum Filatélico and Afinsa left hundreds of thousands of victims in Spain in 2006.
options: True
False
u32l2-10.explanation: They offered attractive returns with stamps. It happened in Spain, not just in films.

u32l3-1.prompt: Put the stages of a pump and dump in order.
options: Members buy and the price shoots up
The price crashes
They post «the signal» in the group
The organisers quietly buy
The organisers sell at the top
u32l3-1.explanation: The organisers win because they get in before you and get out before you.

u32l3-2.prompt: Select the messages typical of a pump and dump.
options: This $0.002 crypto is going x100 this week. Last places in the premium group for €99.
Reminder: crypto-assets are very volatile and you can lose everything you invest.
The ECB leaves interest rates unchanged.
ATTENTION: at 20:00 we announce the coin. Everyone buy at the same time and HOLD. Target x10.
u32l3-2.explanation: A set time for everyone to buy at once, absurd targets and premium fees: pure manipulation.

u32l3-3.prompt: Inflating a price so you can sell to others afterwards is market manipulation and it's banned.
options: True
False
u32l3-3.explanation: It's banned on securities markets and, in the EU, in crypto too under MiCA.

u32l3-4.prompt: Bruno pays €50 a month for a «VIP signals» group. The signal arrives: a crypto has risen 300 % in 10 minutes. What does he do?
options: He buys with borrowed money to make more
He buys now, before it rises further
He doesn't buy: if he's only hearing about it now, he's too late
u32l3-4.explanation: In a pump and dump, the last ones in are the ones who lose.
feedback: That's how manipulation turns into debt.
If it's already up 300 %, the organisers are selling. Bruno would be their buyer.
Good: in a pump, whoever arrives with the signal pays for the party. And maybe the fee isn't worth it either.

u32l3-5.prompt: Which signs give away a pump and dump group? Select all that apply.
options: Very small assets with low trading volume
Explanations with company data and its risks
Targets like «x10» or «x100»
A set time for everyone to buy at once
u32l3-5.explanation: Serious analysis explains risks; manipulation only promises rockets.

u32l3-6.prompt: You buy during the pump at €0.30 with €500. The price drops back to €0.06. How much do you have left?

u32l3-7.prompt: If a price rises very fast, it's because the project is good.
options: True
False
u32l3-7.explanation: It might just be coordinated buying. The price rises as fast as it later crashes.

u32l3-8.prompt: The strategy of inflating a price and selling at the top is called pump and ____.
options: buy
pay
hold
dump

u32l3-9.prompt: In a pump and dump, who usually wins?
options: The organisers, who bought earlier
Those who buy on the signal
Everyone, if nobody sells
u32l3-9.explanation: Some people's profit is the loss of those who arrive later.

u32l3-10.prompt: What do you say to Lumi?
options: Yes! If we all buy, it's bound to go up
It's a pump and dump: the organisers will sell into your purchase
Join in but sell quickly
u32l3-10.explanation: Don't play a game whose rules are set by the winner.
feedback: It goes up… until those who bought earlier sell. And then it falls for everyone else.
Well spotted! Everyone buying «at the same time» is the very definition of manipulation.
Trying to be faster than the people running the game is an almost certain loss.
lines: A Telegram group says a crypto is going x20 tonight 🚀
We just all have to buy at the same time. Shall I join?

u32l4-1.prompt: Select the messages that are phishing or smishing.
options: Your monthly statement is now available in the app.
You have a refund of €312. Enter your card details to receive it.
Your parcel is being held. Pay €1.99 in fees at this link to receive it.
We've detected suspicious access. Verify your identity here within 1 hour or we'll block your account: bit.ly/…
You've made a purchase of €23.40 at a supermarket.
u32l4-1.explanation: Shortened links, urgency, «pay a fee» and «give us your card so we can refund you» are classic signs.

u32l4-2.prompt: What protects you from phishing? Select all that apply.
options: Always going into the app or website by typing the address yourself
Tapping links in text messages to save time
Using a different password for each service
Turning on two-step verification
u32l4-2.explanation: Links in unexpected messages are the most common way in.

u32l4-3.prompt: «Your bank» calls you: to cancel a suspicious purchase they need the code you've just received by text. What do you do?
options: Give them only half the code
Hang up and call the bank's official number myself
Give it to them, they want to help me
u32l4-3.explanation: That code is for authorising a transaction: if you give it out, you're authorising the theft yourself.

u32l4-4.prompt: Match each technique with how it reaches you.
options: Phishing
Smishing
Vishing
Spoofing
u32l4-4.explanation: The channel changes, not the goal: your passwords or your money.
right: By faking the sender or the number

options: Using the same password for everything
Turning on two-step verification
Giving the SMS code to whoever calls you
Logging in to your bank through its official app
Tapping a link to «unblock your account»
u32l4-5.explanation: Safe means going to the official channel yourself; dangerous means following the path they lay out for you.

u32l4-6.prompt: If your bank's real number appears on the screen, the call is definitely from the bank.
options: True
False
u32l4-6.explanation: With spoofing they can fake the number you see. If in doubt, hang up and call them yourself.

u32l4-7.prompt: Quick: which measure means a stolen password isn't enough to log in?
options: Two-step verification
A profile picture
Changing your wallpaper
u32l4-7.explanation: As well as the password, it asks for something only you have, like a code or the app.

u32l4-8.prompt: You tap a link in a text message and enter your broker password. You realise straight away. What do you do first?
options: Change the password from the official app and tell your broker or bank
Delete the text and forget about it
Wait and see if anything happens
u32l4-8.explanation: Act fast: change your passwords, tell the provider and check your transactions.
feedback: Good: you cut off access and the provider can monitor or block transactions.
Deleting the message doesn't delete what they already have.
Every minute counts: they could get in and move your money.

u32l4-9.prompt: Put in order what to do if you've given your bank details to a scammer.
options: Change your passwords
Report it to the police or the Guardia Civil
Check the transactions on your accounts
Call the bank on its official number and block everything
u32l4-9.explanation: First stop the damage, then sort things out and report it.

u32l4-10.prompt: Asking for a password plus a code that only you have is called two-____ verification.
options: key
month
bank
step
u32l4-10.explanation: With it, a stolen password isn't enough.

u32l5-1.prompt: What can an influencer do without CNMV authorisation?
options: Tell you which shares to buy based on your salary and savings
Explain what an ETF or compound interest is
Manage your money
u32l5-1.explanation: Educating is open to anyone; personalised advice requires authorisation.

u32l5-2.prompt: Select the posts that break the rules or are a trap.
options: Today I'm explaining diversification with an example. This isn't an investment recommendation.
#ad This platform is paying me for this video. Remember you can lose money.
DM me your salary and savings and I'll tell you exactly what to buy 💸
This coin is going x50! Link in bio to buy it 🚀🚀 (doesn't say they're paid to promote it)
u32l5-2.explanation: Hidden promotion and personalised advice without authorisation are the two red lines.

u32l5-3.prompt: Can an influencer do this without being an authorised firm?
options: Talk about their portfolio while disclosing their conflicts of interest
Promote crypto without risk warnings
Advertise a product without saying it's an ad
Explain what an index fund is
Tell you what to buy based on your personal situation
u32l5-3.explanation: Education and transparency, yes. Personalised advice and hidden advertising, no.

u32l5-4.prompt: If an influencer writes «this isn't financial advice», they can recommend you buy anything without a problem.
options: True
False
u32l5-4.explanation: The CNMV's guide for finfluencers is clear: that phrase doesn't protect them if in practice they're making recommendations. And crypto advertising must be clear, not misleading and warn about the risks (MiCA).

u32l5-5.prompt: A TikToker with a million followers sells a €997 course to «live off trading in 3 months» plus a signals group. What do you think?
options: I'll buy it, €997 isn't much if I make money fast
If they have that many followers, they must know what they're doing
They make money selling the course, not necessarily from trading
u32l5-5.explanation: When the product is the course, the business is you.
feedback: Promising you can live off trading in 3 months is a red flag, not an offer.
Followers measure popularity, not returns. And their guaranteed income is the course, not the trading.
Exactly. Ask for audited results and be wary of promises about living off trading.

u32l5-6.prompt: Which questions protect you when dealing with a finfluencer? Select all that apply.
options: Do they show their losses too?
How many followers do they have?
Are they rushing me to buy?
Do they make money if I buy?
u32l5-6.explanation: Follower count says nothing about whether they know how to invest.

u32l5-7.prompt: Having lots of followers proves someone knows how to invest.
options: True
False
u32l5-7.explanation: It measures popularity. Plus, we tend to see the wins and not the misses.

u32l5-8.prompt: To give you personalised advice, you need ____ from the CNMV.
options: a course
advertising
a video
authorisation
u32l5-8.explanation: Recommending what to buy based on your situation is a regulated investment service.

u32l5-9.prompt: An influencer earns €0.30 for every person who signs up to a platform with their link and gets 20,000 sign-ups. How much do they earn?
u32l5-9.explanation: 20,000 × 0.30 = €6,000. They earn even if you lose: that's a conflict of interest.

u32l5-10.prompt: What do you say to Lumi?
options: Check whether he's being paid or already owns it, and don't buy in a rush
If he says it so confidently, buy
Buy, but only with half your savings
u32l5-10.explanation: Before listening to someone, ask yourself what they gain from you buying.
feedback: Nice! Conflicts of interest and pressure are two signs to watch for.
Confidence sells, but it isn't right any more often. And maybe he already owns it and wants you to push the price up.
Half your savings because of a video is still far too much.
lines: A YouTuber says you have to buy this share NOW 📈
He's got 2 million subscribers, so he definitely knows.

u32l6-1.prompt: Put in order what to do if you've been scammed.
options: Tell your bank
Report it to the police or the Guardia Civil
Keep all the evidence
Stop sending money
Notify the CNMV
u32l6-1.explanation: First stop the bleeding, then document it and report it.

u32l6-2.prompt: After losing money with an unauthorised firm, a «law firm» messages you: they'll recover your money for an upfront fee of €1,500. What is it?
options: A recovery scam
A useful legal service
A CNMV procedure
u32l6-2.explanation: They take the money upfront and vanish. Often they're the same scammers.

u32l6-3.prompt: Telling your bank as soon as possible can help to try to stop a transfer or block your card.
options: True
False
u32l6-3.explanation: It doesn't always work, but the sooner, the better your chances.

u32l6-4.prompt: Match each situation with where to go.
options: You've been scammed by an unauthorised firm
Unresolved problem with your bank
Unresolved problem with an authorised broker
Questions about an online scam
u32l6-4.explanation: Each body covers a different type of problem.
right: CNMV, after complaining to the firm
Police or Guardia Civil, and notify the CNMV

u32l6-5.prompt: The platform you invested with says that, to withdraw your «profits», you first have to pay €2,000 in taxes. What do you do?
options: Take out a loan to pay it
Pay nothing more, keep evidence and report it
Pay: that way I'll get it all back
u32l6-5.explanation: «Pay to withdraw» is the ultimate sign of a scam.
feedback: You'd be adding debt to the scam.
Good: no legal firm charges taxes upfront to let you withdraw your money.
It's the last trick before they disappear: next they'll ask for another «fee».

u32l6-6.prompt: What evidence is worth keeping? Select all that apply.
options: Transfer receipts
Nothing, so you can forget about it sooner
The website address and its name
Screenshots of chats and messages
u32l6-6.explanation: Without evidence, reporting it and making any claim are much harder.

u32l6-7.prompt: If you've been scammed, it's better not to report it out of embarrassment.
options: True
False
u32l6-7.explanation: Reporting helps investigations and warns others. It happens to people of all ages and professions.

u32l6-8.prompt: Legitimate help or a second scam?
options: INCIBE's 017 gives you free guidance
Complaining to your bank's customer service department
The police or Guardia Civil take your report
A «lawyer» who contacts you first and asks you to pay upfront
A website that claims to recover stolen crypto in exchange for a fee
u32l6-8.explanation: Anyone who contacts you unprompted and charges you upfront to recover your money is suspicious.

u32l6-9.prompt: You have a problem with an authorised broker. Where do you complain first?
options: On its social media
Straight to court
To the broker's own customer service department
u32l6-9.explanation: It's the mandatory first step; if they don't respond or don't side with you, you can go to the CNMV.

u32l6-10.explanation: 112 is for emergencies and 091 is the Policía Nacional; 016 supports victims of gender-based violence.
